documents.title: Syllabus Minimum Requirements Policy (Artificial Intelligence (AI) Usage section)
documents.summary: The university's syllabus minimum requirements policy, revised by Faculty Senate in June 2026, adds an AI usage section. Every syllabus must include an AI usage policy for students, while whether AI is permitted or prohibited is left to each instructor. The rest of the policy covers non-AI syllabus elements.

units.anchor: All course syllabi must include an AI usage policy
units.policy: All course syllabi must include an AI usage policy that communicates expectations for student use of artificial intelligence.

units.anchor: Determination of permitted or prohibited AI use remains at the discretion of the instructor.
Faculty Senate (add the AI statement)
units.policy: The Faculty Senate revised the syllabus minimum requirements policy on 06/11/2026 to add the AI statement requirement.

documents.title: University Guidance on the Use of Generative AI in Teaching and Learning (memo to faculty)
documents.summary: A September 2025 memo from the Senior Vice Provost announcing workgroup-developed university guidance on generative AI in teaching. It strongly encourages instructors to follow the instructor guidance and to add a tailored GenAI syllabus statement, and anticipates that the statement will become a syllabus requirement. It lists support resources and the workgroup members.

documents.title: Guidance for AI Use in Teaching and Learning
tiers: Minor Uses Permitted for AI Tools
AI Use Encouraged and Fully Permitted
Specific Expectations and Notes for AI Use
documents.summary: The university's official instructor guidance on AI in teaching, plus a syllabus statement template. It permits instructor AI use for materials and for initial review and feedback using only OSU-approved tools, requires human review and grading, restricts what student data may be entered into unapproved tools, and requires a syllabus AI policy at instructor discretion. The template offers four icon-labeled tiers (Do Not Use to Fully Permitted) plus a custom option and tells instructors what details to include.

units.anchor: integrating generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) into teaching and learning offers tremendous possibilities
that integration must reflect our shared commitments to human cognition and creativity, academic integrity
units.policy: Integrating AI into teaching and learning must reflect shared commitments to human cognition and creativity, academic integrity, and inclusive excellence.

units.anchor: This guidance supports faculty autonomy and intellectual freedom in designing engaged learning experiences
units.policy: The guidance supports faculty autonomy and intellectual freedom in designing learning experiences that may include AI use.

units.anchor: protecting the privacy and security of individual and institutional data
units.policy: The guidance aims to maintain transparency, uphold ethical responsibilities as educators, and protect the privacy and security of individual and institutional data.

units.anchor: refers to a broad set of advanced digital technologies - rooted in statistics, computer science
units.policy: AI refers to a broad set of advanced digital technologies, rooted in statistics, computer science, and cognitive psychology, that enable machines to perform complex tasks beyond the reach of traditional programming.

units.anchor: represents a subset of software tools that use questions, prompts, and other inputs
units.policy: Generative AI is a subset of software tools that use prompts and other inputs to generate human-like output such as responses, documents, software code, or designs.

units.anchor: GenAI includes both standalone offerings, such as ChatGPT, and offerings that are embedded
units.policy: GenAI includes both standalone offerings, such as ChatGPT, and offerings embedded in other software, such as Microsoft 365's Copilot.

units.anchor: You are welcome to use AI tools.
units.policy: Instructors and staff are welcome to use AI tools.

units.anchor: instructors and staff are encouraged to utilize
units.policy: Instructors and staff are encouraged to use OSU's Recommended and Approved AI tools whenever possible.

units.anchor: In some cases, as described below, OSU's Recommended and Approved AI tools are required.

units.policy: OSU employees may explore other AI tools provided no confidential, sensitive, or student information (e.g., personally identifiable information, student or employee records, research data) is included.

units.anchor: (UIT) is the authority on and maintains the list
units.policy: OSU's University Information and Technology (UIT) is the authority on and maintains the list of OSU's Recommended and Approved AI tools.

units.anchor: Enhanced data privacy,
units.frag_start: Using OSU's Recommended and Approved AI tools
units.frag_end: Access to technical support systems, and Institutional protections.
units.policy: Using OSU's Recommended and Approved AI tools ensures integrated security measures, standardized protocols, enhanced data privacy, access to technical support, and institutional protections.

units.anchor: input student work into any AI tools or applications that are not approved by OSU
units.policy: To protect student privacy, meet legal obligations, and uphold enterprise security, instructors may not input student work into any AI tools or applications not approved by OSU.

units.anchor: All course syllabi must include an AI usage policy
units.policy: All course syllabi must include an AI usage policy that communicates expectations for student use of artificial intelligence.

units.anchor: Determination of permitted or prohibited AI use remains at the discretion of the instructor.
encouraged to identify in a syllabus statement if AI or AI tools will be used
units.policy: Instructors are strongly encouraged to identify in a syllabus statement if AI will be used to substantially create, augment, or refine instructional materials, or to provide initial review of student work, draft feedback, or score materials with a rubric.

units.anchor: may use AI to create, augment, or refine instructional materials, assignments, or assessments
units.policy: Instructors may use AI to create, augment, or refine instructional materials, assignments, or assessments.

units.anchor: instructors are strongly encouraged to disclose in a syllabus statement their AI usage
units.policy: If an instructor uses AI in a substantial way to create, augment, or refine instructional materials, the instructor is strongly encouraged to disclose that AI usage in a syllabus statement.

units.anchor: required to review instructional materials created by AI
units.policy: Instructors are required to review instructional materials created by AI to ensure the highest quality, accuracy, and appropriateness.

units.anchor: may direct students to use AI applications and tools
units.policy: Instructors may direct students to use AI applications and tools as part of their learning in the course.

units.anchor: AI tools that are not on the OSU Recommended and Approved list may be required
units.policy: Instructors may require AI tools not on the OSU Recommended and Approved list, as long as the assigned activities do not require students to enter their own creative works, sensitive data, or personally identifiable information.

units.anchor: tools if the student is required to enter their own creative works, sensitive data
units.policy: Instructors must use OSU Recommended and Approved AI tools if students are required to enter their own creative works, sensitive data, or personally identifiable information into the AI tool.

units.anchor: When possible, instructors are encouraged to use OSU Recommended and Approved AI tools
units.policy: When possible, instructors are encouraged to use OSU Recommended and Approved AI tools as part of the requirements for course activities and assignments.

units.anchor: initial review of student work, draft feedback, or score materials against a rubric
units.policy: Instructors may use OSU Recommended and Approved AI tools to provide an initial review of student work, draft feedback, or score materials against a rubric.
units.policy_type: NEW:Instructor AI for feedback and grading

units.anchor: instructors are ultimately responsible for assigning grades based on their human evaluation
units.policy: Instructors are ultimately responsible for assigning grades based on their human evaluation of student work.

units.anchor: strongly encouraged to disclose to students in their syllabus statement if they will use
units.policy: Instructors are strongly encouraged to disclose to students in their syllabus statement if they will use approved AI tools to provide initial review of student work, draft feedback, or score materials with a rubric.

units.anchor: only OSU Recommended and Approved AI tools may be used to provide such review
units.policy: Only OSU Recommended and Approved AI tools may be used to provide initial review, feedback, or scoring of student work.

units.anchor: may not input student work to any AI tools or applications that are not recommended
units.policy: Due to privacy and data security concerns, instructors may not input student work to any AI tools or applications that are not recommended and approved by OSU.

units.anchor: required to review feedback for students
units.policy: Instructors are required to review feedback for students created by AI to ensure quality, accuracy, and appropriateness for the course and the student.

units.anchor: should only be used for coursework in ways that adhere to individual instructor guidelines
units.policy: AI tools should only be used for coursework in ways that adhere to individual instructor guidelines.

units.anchor: When AI use is permitted, care must be taken to use these tools responsibly.
Instructors differ in their adoption of and approach to AI tools
students are responsible for reviewing individual course policies and understanding appropriate use in each course
Please contact the instructor if you have questions about specific AI tools
units.policy: Students should contact the instructor with questions about specific AI tools and the allowable usage of AI in the course.

units.anchor: Choose one of the options below to copy/paste here

units.policy: Under the Do Not Use option, using any AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Copilot, Claude) to generate or edit any portion of the substance of student work is not permitted unless explicitly noted in the assignment instructions.

units.policy: Under the Do Not Use option, AI embedded in everyday tools (Word grammar check, PowerPoint design suggestions, search engines) is tolerated as limited non-substantive support, and no AI use beyond these is allowed.

units.policy: Under the Minor Uses Permitted option, students may use AI in minor ways the instructor lists, unless otherwise specified in the assignment, and may not use AI for the uses the instructor lists as not allowed.

units.anchor: Always review individual assignments for specific instructions.
attribute that use by putting that language in quotation marks and adding a citation
units.policy: Optionally, instructors may require that students using language generated by an AI tool attribute it by putting it in quotation marks and adding a citation.

units.anchor: students are permitted to integrate AI into some of the substantive work of the course
units.policy: Under the AI Tools Integrated by Assignment option, students are permitted to integrate AI into some of the substantive work of the course.

units.anchor: Review individual assignments to determine permissible uses.
you should be able to demonstrate how you contributed to the work you submit
units.policy: Unless otherwise noted, students should be able to demonstrate how they contributed to the work they submit for an assignment.

if one of the above icons does not suit your policy

documents.title: CTL Guidance for Syllabus Statements about AI Use
documents.summary: A CTL Canvas page helping instructors write a course AI syllabus statement under the new syllabus requirement. It argues that total prohibition is impractical and detectors are unreliable, recommends trying AI tools and consulting colleagues first, points to the university's tiered categories and template, and encourages instructors to disclose their own AI use, align assignments with the policy, and discuss it with students throughout the term.

units.anchor: course syllabi must include an AI usage policy that communicates expectations for student use
units.policy: All course syllabi must include an AI usage policy that communicates expectations for student use of artificial intelligence.

units.anchor: Determination of permitted or prohibited AI use remains at the discretion of the instructor.
supports an ethic of transparency around the use of generative AI in teaching and learning
units.policy: CTL supports an ethic of transparency around the use of generative AI in teaching and learning.

units.anchor: encourages you to develop and share a course-level AI policy statement in your syllabus
units.policy: CTL encourages instructors to develop and share a course-level AI policy statement in their syllabus.

units.anchor: Consider that AI is ubiquitous and embedded in many writing tools
units.policy: Instructors should consider that AI is ubiquitous and embedded in many writing tools (e.g., Grammarly, online translators, Google Docs autocomplete).

units.anchor: AI tools are also widely used to generate visual and audio content.
Completely prohibiting the use of AI is increasingly impractical
AI use is not accurately detectable
we do not recommend mentioning them in syllabus statements or using them as a basis

several categories of course AI policies, ranging from no AI use to fully accepted
units.policy: OSU AI guidance identifies several categories of course AI policies, ranging from no AI use to fully accepted and encouraged AI use, with icons, sample language, and a template.

units.anchor: You are encouraged to modify the language to fit your approach

units.anchor: Betsey has generously given blanket permission to OSU faculty who would like to adapt it

units.anchor: OSU teaching faculty are invited to share your AI-related syllabus statements

documents.title: Generative AI Guidelines for Ecampus Course Development
documents.summary: Ecampus guidelines for faculty and staff using generative AI when developing online courses. Ecampus encourages AI use that streamlines development but asks for careful consideration of uses affecting authorship, instructor presence, or interaction (e.g., simulated instructor voice, chatbots, AI grading). It requires approved tools, full faculty review, clear labeling, and a syllabus acknowledgment for substantial AI-made content.

units.anchor: Ecampus encourages AI use in ways that advance innovation and streamline course development
units.policy: Ecampus encourages AI use in ways that advance innovation and streamline course development while upholding the authenticity and quality of the student learning experience.

units.anchor: Ecampus will adhere to OSU's Guidance for AI Use in Teaching and Learning
units.policy: When faculty or Ecampus staff use generative AI in course development, Ecampus will adhere to OSU's Guidance for AI Use in Teaching and Learning and the Ecampus-specific guidelines.

units.anchor: should carefully consider the use of generative AI, either routine or experimental
units.policy: Ecampus staff and faculty partners should carefully consider any routine or experimental generative AI use that significantly affects authorship, instructor presence, or student interaction in the course.

units.anchor: creating new learning content that is not originally authored by the faculty
units.policy: Uses requiring careful consideration include creating new learning content not originally authored by the faculty.

units.anchor: generating or simulating the instructor's voice, image, or persona in learning content
units.policy: Uses requiring careful consideration include generating or simulating the instructor's voice, image, or persona in learning content.

units.anchor: creating course chat bots
units.policy: Uses requiring careful consideration include creating course chatbots.

units.anchor: using tools that promote AI-assisted grading
units.policy: Uses requiring careful consideration include tools that promote AI-assisted grading (e.g., auto-grading in Perusall or Gradescope), due to potential impact on teaching quality and regular-and-substantive interaction requirements.
units.policy_type: NEW:Instructor AI for feedback and grading

units.anchor: using generative AI in ways that substantially shape the course's content
units.policy: Uses requiring careful consideration include using generative AI in ways that substantially shape the course's content, instructional approach, or delivery.

units.anchor: Ecampus staff will discuss implications of using generative AI with the faculty developer
units.policy: Ecampus staff will discuss the implications of using generative AI with the faculty developer in the desired use case.

units.anchor: we will consider issues and risks that are outlined in the AI Decision Tree
units.policy: For all uses, Ecampus will consider the issues and risks outlined in the AI Decision Tree to guide the decision to use AI.

units.anchor: Any use of voice automation should follow the three recommendations
units.policy: Any use of voice automation should follow the three recommendations in the Ecampus Voice Automation and AI document, applying professional judgement case by case.

units.anchor: being transparent when it's employed
units.policy: Voice automation recommendations emphasize being transparent when voice automation is employed.

units.anchor: Ecampus multimedia staff will not use AI tools to produce critical course content in full.
Ecampus staff will use only OSU's approved Gen AI tools when working with faculty-created instructional
units.policy: Ecampus staff will use only OSU's approved GenAI tools when working with faculty-created instructional materials for course development.

units.anchor: Use of non-OSU approved AI tools requires instructor permission.
require full review by the faculty developer, who will be accountable for its accuracy
units.policy: Any AI-generated content used in a course will require full review by the faculty developer, who will be accountable for its accuracy.

units.anchor: Learning objects created with generative AI will be labeled clearly.
the label should appear within the media itself
units.policy: When AI-created learning objects are used in video or media that could be used outside the course, the label should appear within the media itself.

units.anchor: will acknowledge this with a syllabus statement at minimum
units.policy: Courses that use AI to create, augment, or refine content in a substantial way will acknowledge this with a syllabus statement at minimum.

units.anchor: should align with the seven principles outlined in our Ecampus AI ethics statement
units.policy: Any future, yet-to-be-defined use of generative AI in course development should align with the seven principles of the Ecampus AI ethics statement.

units.anchor: may require department approval
units.policy: Future, yet-to-be-defined uses of generative AI in course development may require department approval.

documents.unit: College of Engineering (Academic Integrity Resources for Faculty)
documents.title: AI Chatbot Policy Example
documents.summary: A College of Engineering example course policy offered to faculty as an academic-integrity resource. It permits AI chatbots like a library resource for debugging help, understanding code, verifying algorithms, small code snippets, and parts of written reports, but forbids having AI write software or documents and warns of detection and integrity consequences. Much of it argues from industry practice and skill development.

units.anchor: You ARE allowed to use ChatGPT, Google Bard, Bing AI, or similar AI chatbots
units.policy: Students are allowed to use ChatGPT, Google Bard, Bing AI, or similar AI chatbots as they would a library resource.

units.anchor: similar AI chatbots as you would a library resource
units.policy: AI chatbots are to be used as one would use a library resource.

units.anchor: use ChatGPT to find solutions for errors the same way you would use Stackoverflow
units.policy: Students may use ChatGPT to find solutions for errors the same way they would use Stack Overflow or other Internet resources.

units.anchor: to understand and improve software you are developing
units.policy: Students may use AI chatbots to understand and improve software they are developing.

units.anchor: You ARE allowed to use AI chatbots to verify algorithms.
You will learn more if you develop your algorithms yourself
units.policy: Students learn more by developing algorithms themselves and using a chatbot to verify them than by having ChatGPT generate the algorithms.

units.anchor: the critical thinking skills that AI cannot replace
units.policy: Developing algorithms oneself builds understanding of the problem and critical thinking skills that AI cannot replace.

units.anchor: there are guaranteed to be problems for which AI cannot propose algorithms or solutions
units.policy: In a career, there are guaranteed to be problems for which AI cannot propose algorithms or solutions.

units.anchor: you will be unable to deliver the value your employer expects from a practicing engineer
units.policy: Students who have not developed the critical thinking skills to develop solution algorithms on their own will be unable to deliver the value employers expect from a practicing engineer.

units.anchor: You ARE allowed to use AI chatbots for small snippets of code
units.policy: Students are allowed to use AI chatbots for small snippets of code, as they would online references like Reddit or language-specific websites.

units.anchor: do not introduce software license restrictions or the possibility of copyright, trademark, trade secret
units.policy: In industry, small snippets from any source must not introduce software license restrictions or possible copyright, trademark, trade secret, or confidentiality violations.

units.anchor: you should be cautiously selective about the number and size of code snippets
units.policy: One should be cautiously selective about the number and size of code snippets included in commercial products, whether from programming websites or an AI chatbot.

units.anchor: It is wiser and safer to adapt the principles demonstrated in those snippets
units.policy: It is wiser and safer to adapt the principles in snippets to one's own code and context rather than pasting something into the code verbatim.

units.anchor: Practicing this kind of appropriate use as a student will help establish a foundation
units.policy: Practicing appropriate use as a student helps establish career behaviors consistent with an employer's code of ethics.

units.anchor: allowed to use chatbots in manners similar to the above for generating written reports
units.policy: Students are allowed to use chatbots in similar ways for generating written reports or other creative elements, but not whole blocks or reports.

units.anchor: the same possibilities of not learning to think, write, or be creative
units.policy: Using chatbots for writing carries the risk of not learning to think, write, or be creative on one's own, and being less able to meet employer expectations.

units.anchor: You should never blindly submit something based on AI chatbots without using critical thinking
units.policy: Students should never blindly submit something based on AI chatbots without using critical thinking and good judgment to assess the correctness and validity of the results.

units.anchor: You won't get proper credit for work based on incorrect or invalid output
units.policy: Students will not get proper credit for work based on incorrect or invalid output from AI or any other source.

units.anchor: apply that same level of discernment to the output of AI chatbots
units.policy: Students should assess the validity of AI chatbot output with the same discernment they apply to any tool or information source.

units.anchor: abdicating your creative thought processes to any tool won't necessarily grow your abilities
units.policy: Abdicating creative thought processes to any tool won't necessarily grow one's ability to think creatively.

units.anchor: be thoughtful and judicious about how much you use these or any tools
units.policy: Students should be thoughtful and judicious about how much they use these tools as a replacement for their work rather than a supplement to it.

units.anchor: send me an email explaining your planned use
units.policy: Students unsure whether an intended chatbot use is allowed should email the instructor explaining the planned use, and the instructor will say whether it is allowable in the course and in industry.

units.anchor: allowed to use AI chatbots to simply write your software for you
units.policy: Students are not allowed to use AI chatbots to simply write their software or their documents for them.

units.anchor: we instructors have tools to identify code and documents that were generated
units.policy: Instructors have tools to identify code and documents that were generated.

units.anchor: Any student that submits generated responses will be subject to an Academic Integrity violation.
Our goal at OSU is to prepare you for a career in industry
units.policy: OSU aims to prepare students for industry careers that require solving problems through critical thinking and following industry norms for high-integrity, ethical behavior.

units.anchor: You will not be expected to let a tool do all your work for you
units.policy: In industry, students will not be expected to let a tool do all their work without understanding the problem-solving process and judging whether results are credible.

units.anchor: that's good preparation for being in industry with a broad toolkit at your disposal
units.policy: Using AI chatbots for the allowed purposes to understand their capabilities and limitations is good preparation for industry.

units.anchor: you will limit your career opportunities
units.policy: Using AI chatbots to do one's work and skate by with minimal effort limits career opportunities.

units.anchor: will continue to increase in the fields of software engineering and computer science
units.policy: Use of AI and machine learning tools will continue to increase in software engineering and computer science.

units.anchor: they were not designed to be learning tools, or to understand the context or nuances
units.policy: AI language models were not designed to be learning tools or to understand the context or nuances of a particular software problem.

units.anchor: learn and develop a strong foundation in the fundamental principles and concepts of software development
units.policy: It is still important to develop a strong foundation in the fundamental principles of software development, so as to adapt to and use new tools effectively and responsibly.

documents.unit: School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS)
documents.title: Guidance on Drafting AI Use Policies
documents.summary: EECS's June 2026 school-wide floor for AI use across courses, leaving course-specific rules to faculty. It sets a fallback (only grammar help when a syllabus is silent), brings IDE assistants like Copilot and Cursor under the policy, requires disclosure at submission and in-work attribution of AI-generated code, and requires students to explain and defend their work. It also covers faculty AI use for materials and feedback, a research section with disclosure tiers, and integrity guidance that rejects AI detectors while accepting MOSS/JPlag and behavioral evidence. Appendix A defines nine use categories applied per assignment.

units.anchor: AI tools have become a part of how work is being done
units.policy: AI tools have become part of how work is done in industry, in research, and increasingly in the classroom.

units.anchor: This statement establishes shared expectations for AI use across EECS courses
units.policy: The statement establishes shared expectations for AI use across EECS courses so as to set clear expectations.

units.anchor: individual faculty will set course-specific rules, this document provides the common floor and vocabulary
units.policy: Individual faculty set course-specific rules, while this document provides the common floor and vocabulary.

units.anchor: developed using the OSU College of Science Artificial Intelligence Guidelines (September 2025)
units.policy: The statement adapts the OSU College of Science AI Guidelines (September 2025) to EECS and aligns with CTL guidance and the AI@OregonState guidelines.

units.anchor: Where those documents conflict with this one, OSU policy governs.
this document will be updated to align with it when finalized
units.policy: A College of Engineering AI policy is in development, and this document will be updated to align with it when finalized.

units.anchor: Initial version. Developed by Anita Sarma, Associate Head, EECS
units.policy: The policy keeps a version history; the initial version (June 2026) was developed by the EECS Associate Head.

units.anchor: GenAI systems are built on foundation models, including large language models (LLMs)
units.policy: GenAI, the category this policy addresses, comprises systems built on foundation models (LLMs, VLMs, small language models) that generate human-like text, code, images, audio, or other media.

units.anchor: GenAI systems include standalone tools, agentic systems, multi-modal pipelines, and automated workflows
units.policy: GenAI systems include standalone tools, agentic systems, multi-modal pipelines, and automated workflows that incorporate these models.

units.anchor: it means GenAI unless otherwise specified
units.policy: Where the document refers to 'AI,' it means GenAI unless otherwise specified.

units.anchor: Faculty may use GenAI to create, augment, or refine instructional materials, assignments, or assessments.
Faculty are required to review instructional materials created by GenAI
units.policy: Faculty are required to review instructional materials created by GenAI to ensure the highest quality, accuracy, and appropriateness.

units.anchor: they are strongly encouraged to disclose in a syllabus statement their AI usage
units.policy: Faculty who use AI substantially to create, augment, or refine instructional materials are strongly encouraged to disclose that usage in a syllabus statement.

units.anchor: Routine grammar assistance, search features, or autocomplete do not require disclosure.
tools to provide an initial review of student work, draft feedback, or score materials
units.policy: Faculty may use OSU Recommended and Approved GenAI tools to provide an initial review of student work, draft feedback, or score materials against a rubric.
units.policy_type: NEW:Instructor AI for feedback and grading

units.anchor: Grades must reflect the faculty member's own evaluation of student work.
Faculty must disclose in their syllabus statement when GenAI tools will be used
units.policy: Faculty must disclose in their syllabus statement when GenAI tools will be used in any part of the grading or feedback process.

units.anchor: Only OSU Recommended and Approved tools may be used when assessing student work
units.policy: Only OSU Recommended and Approved tools may be used when assessing student work, as these carry the data privacy and institutional protections required for student records.

units.anchor: Faculty must explain their GenAI use policy in their course.
Students may not recognize that AI-assisted features in common development tools constitute GenAI use
units.policy: Students may not recognize that AI-assisted features in common development tools count as GenAI use under this policy.

units.anchor: Students may use AI tools when course policies explicitly permit it.
When no policy is stated, only routine grammar corrections are allowed
units.policy: When no course AI policy is stated, only routine grammar corrections are allowed.

units.anchor: any other AI use must be arranged with the instructor of record before using it
units.policy: When no policy is stated, any AI use other than routine grammar correction must be arranged with the instructor of record before using it on coursework.

units.anchor: Search features and autocomplete do not require arrangement or disclosure.
students are expected to be able to explain and defend any work they submit
units.policy: Regardless of what AI use is permitted, students are expected to be able to explain and defend any work they submit.

units.anchor: AI use exists on a spectrum from light assistance at one end
units.policy: AI use exists on a spectrum from light assistance to full content generation, defined by the Appendix A category taxonomy.

units.anchor: Course policies will specify which categories apply to each assignment.
AI embedded in tools you already use counts as GenAI use under this policy.
GitHub Copilot, VS Code or Cursor assistants, and similar IDE features fall within this policy
units.policy: GitHub Copilot, VS Code or Cursor assistants, and similar IDE features fall within this policy even when they feel like autocomplete.

units.anchor: that applies to embedded tools as well as standalone ones
units.policy: When a course restricts or requires disclosure of GenAI use, that applies to embedded tools as well as standalone ones.

units.anchor: When you use AI on permitted work, disclose it at the point of submission
identify the tool, the type of interaction, and what portion of the final work
units.policy: The disclosure must identify the tool, the type of interaction, and what portion of the final work the AI contributed.

units.anchor: For agentic tools, describe the task given and the extent of its autonomy.
A one-line disclosure is sufficient in most cases.
For guidance on citing AI tools in APA, MLA, and Chicago formats
units.policy: Guidance on citing AI tools in APA, MLA, and Chicago formats is in the OSU Library's GenAI guidance.

units.anchor: that engagement may carry its own AI use restrictions beyond what the syllabus states
units.policy: Work with an external sponsor or industry partner may carry its own AI use restrictions beyond what the syllabus states.
units.policy_type: NEW:Defer to external venue and sponsor rules

units.anchor: Check with your instructor before using AI tools on sponsor-related deliverables.
Recording the instructor or other students is permitted only when the instructor allows it
units.policy: Recording the instructor or other students is permitted only when the instructor allows it or as a documented disability accommodation (Oregon is an all-party consent state).

units.anchor: upload a recording of a lecture, discussion, or any other person to an AI tool
units.policy: Students must not upload a recording of a lecture, discussion, or any other person to an AI tool without the instructor's permission.

units.anchor: This section applies to research work by EECS graduate students, undergraduate researchers, and faculty
units.policy: The research section applies to research by EECS graduate students, undergraduate researchers, and faculty, including theses, dissertations, manuscripts, proposals, reports, and committee documents.

units.anchor: Where venue, sponsor, IRB, or funder rules are stricter, those rules govern.
units.policy_type: NEW:Defer to external venue and sponsor rules

units.anchor: venues (conferences, journals, funders, committees) set their own AI rules, which are changing quickly
units.policy: In research, the unit of evaluation is the intellectual contribution, and venues set their own AI rules, which are changing quickly.
units.policy_type: NEW:Defer to external venue and sponsor rules

units.anchor: Treat venue rules as the primary constraint and this policy as the floor.
units.policy_type: NEW:Defer to external venue and sponsor rules

units.anchor: The major advisor sets AI use norms for research conducted under their supervision.
AI use expectations should be set with the full committee and documented early
units.policy: For thesis and dissertation work, AI use expectations should be set with the full committee and documented early, such as at the program of study meeting.

units.anchor: AI tools may be used for grammar checking, search, and autocomplete without prior approval
units.policy: Where no research AI norms have been set, AI tools may be used for grammar checking, search, and autocomplete without prior approval.

units.anchor: any substantive use requires prior approval
units.policy: Where no research AI norms have been set, any substantive AI use requires prior approval.

units.anchor: The final product must be the researcher's, reviewed and revised to that standard.
Blindly using or following AI output is itself an integrity concern.
The researcher is the author and accountable for the work.
AI fabricates citations, misstates prior work, produces plausible but incorrect analyses
units.policy: AI fabricates citations, misstates prior work, produces plausible but incorrect analyses, and can reproduce text from existing sources without attribution.

units.anchor: Every factual claim, citation, quantitative result, and code path must be independently verified
AI-assisted text should be checked for similarity to existing work
must be the researcher's own
units.policy: The intellectual content (research question, design choices, analysis decisions, interpretation) must be the researcher's own.

units.anchor: Treat AI as a tool; authorship belongs to the researcher.
Researchers must be able to explain and justify any submitted text, analysis, or code
units.policy: Researchers must be able to explain and justify any submitted text, analysis, or code to an advisor, committee, or reviewer.

units.anchor: Follow venue rules first.
units.policy: In research, follow venue rules on AI disclosure first.
units.policy_type: NEW:Defer to external venue and sponsor rules

units.anchor: most major venues now require disclosure of substantive AI use, and some prohibit specific uses
units.policy: ACM, IEEE, NeurIPS, NIH, NSF, and most major venues now require disclosure of substantive AI use, and some prohibit specific uses.
units.policy_type: NEW:Defer to external venue and sponsor rules

units.anchor: disclose substantive use in methods, acknowledgments, or an authorcontribution statement: tool, task type, and scope
units.policy: Where venue rules are silent, researchers disclose substantive AI use in methods, acknowledgments, or an author-contribution statement, giving tool, task type, and scope.

units.anchor: Disclose any image-editing or imagegeneration process specifically.
The same expectation applies to documents submitted to examination committees.
units.policy: The research disclosure expectation also applies to documents submitted to examination committees.

units.anchor: Do not upload sensitive or confidential material to nonapproved AI tools.
other people's unpublished work, such as a coauthor's draft or a collaborator's code
units.policy: Material not to upload to non-approved AI tools includes proprietary or sponsor-restricted material, identifiable human-subjects information, and others' unpublished work used without their permission.

units.anchor: Sponsor agreements and IRB protocols may restrict AI use further.
units.policy_type: NEW:Defer to external venue and sponsor rules

units.anchor: cannot be reused verbatim in later documents even when the words are the researcher's own
units.policy: Prior work published under copyright transfer cannot be reused verbatim even in the researcher's own words; AI assistance does not change this, so rewrite, paraphrase with citation, or obtain permission.

units.anchor: It is recommended that students run a similarity check to other existing works
units.policy: Students are recommended to run a similarity check (e.g., Draft Coach) on all documents submitted to examination committees.

units.anchor: Students should escalate disagreements to the Associate Head of Graduate Programs (AHGP).
The school of EECS expects every course syllabus to include an AI statement.
reflects OSU's strong encouragement and anticipated future requirement
units.policy: The syllabus AI statement is a school expectation reflecting OSU's strong encouragement and anticipated future requirement.

units.anchor: with tiered icons and language covering the full range from prohibited to fully permitted use
units.policy: CTL provides a GenAI syllabus statement template with tiered icons and language covering the full range from prohibited to fully permitted use.

units.anchor: The syllabus statement should cover the Student AI use policy
units.policy: The syllabus statement should cover what students are and are not permitted to do with AI across the course.

units.anchor: AI use permissions should align with course learning objectives so that grades reflect
units.policy: AI use permissions should align with course learning objectives so that grades reflect actual student mastery of those objectives.

units.anchor: Learning outcome assessment should require independent demonstration of the underlying skill
units.policy: Learning outcome assessment should require independent demonstration of the underlying skill, and the AI policy for that assessment must reflect that expectation.

units.anchor: Assignments that deviate from the course default, tighter or looser, should say so explicitly
units.policy: Assignments that deviate from the course AI default, tighter or looser, should say so explicitly in the assignment prompt.

units.anchor: Assignments that follow the course default need no additional statement.
A sample syllabus table mapping these categories to course-specific examples and permissions is available
Syllabi must not specify grade sanctions for academic misconduct
sanction determinations belong to the College Hearing Officer
Faculty who need support drafting syllabus statements or designing AI-resilient assignments can request a consultation
Unauthorized AI use may constitute plagiarism, cheating, and / or falsification
units.policy: Unauthorized AI use may constitute plagiarism, cheating, and/or falsification under OSU's Code of Student Conduct.

units.anchor: presenting AI-generated content as your own work without disclosure
units.policy: Plagiarism includes presenting AI-generated content as one's own work without disclosure.

units.anchor: code is incorporated into a submission, it must be attributed in the work itself
units.policy: Where AI-generated text or code is incorporated into a submission, it must be attributed in the work itself.

units.anchor: Submission-level disclosure does not substitute for in-text attribution.
using AI to complete an assignment without prior authorization from your instructor
units.policy: Cheating includes using AI to complete an assignment without prior authorization from the instructor.

units.anchor: using AI to create counterfeit citations, interview responses, or research results
units.policy: Fabrication includes using AI to create counterfeit citations, interview responses, or research results.

units.anchor: faculty should follow the formal reporting process outlined in
units.policy: Faculty facing AI-related academic misconduct under the Code of Student Conduct should follow the formal reporting process in the Academic Integrity resources.

units.anchor: cannot serve as sole evidence in a misconduct case
units.policy: AI detection tools are not reliable indicators of AI use and cannot serve as sole evidence in a misconduct case.

units.anchor: These tools have been shown to produce inaccurate results and can lead to biases
units.policy: AI detection tools produce inaccurate results and can lead to biases in determining culpability.

units.anchor: A high AI probability score can encourage additional scrutiny but does not definitively prove
units.policy: A high AI probability score can prompt additional scrutiny but does not definitively prove a student used AI.

units.anchor: Faculty may not submit student work to AI detection tools that are not OSU Recommended
units.policy: Faculty may not submit student work to AI detection tools that are not OSU Recommended and Approved, as this may violate data privacy requirements.

units.anchor: Code similarity tools such as MOSS and JPlag occupy different evidentiary ground.
units.policy: Code similarity tools such as MOSS and JPlag detect similarity between submissions and have an established record in academic integrity cases, unlike AI detectors.

units.anchor: legitimate evidence of potential misconduct and may be submitted as part of a case
units.policy: A MOSS flag is not proof of AI use specifically, but it is legitimate evidence of potential misconduct and may be submitted as part of a case.

units.anchor: Faculty should not conflate code similarity findings with AI detection findings.
faculty should rely on the behavioral evidence described below
units.policy: For ECE and other non-software courses where similarity tools do not apply, faculty should rely on behavioral evidence.

units.anchor: Faculty building a misconduct case should document behavioral evidence
units.policy: Faculty building a misconduct case should document behavioral evidence such as inconsistent style, off-prompt responses, fabricated facts or references, or similarity to AI output for the prompt.

units.anchor: These categories apply across work products: text, code, simulations, circuit designs, lab reports
units.policy: The AI use categories apply across work products: text, code, simulations, circuit designs, lab reports, and other outputs.

units.anchor: For non-software courses, faculty should interpret and apply them in the context of their discipline.
using AI to explain difficult concepts, assignment prompts, or course material
units.policy: The Clarification category is using AI to explain difficult concepts, assignment prompts, or course material.

units.anchor: brainstorming research topics, thesis statements, design concepts, or approaches
units.policy: The Idea generation category is brainstorming research topics, thesis statements, design concepts, or approaches.

units.anchor: condensing readings, lecture notes, or other materials to highlight key points
units.policy: The Summarization category is condensing readings, lecture notes, or other materials to highlight key points.

units.anchor: does not include submitting AI-translated text as original work without disclosure
units.policy: The Translation category is using AI to translate prompts, sources, or one's own drafted text, and does not include submitting AI-translated text as original work without disclosure.

units.anchor: checking grammar, tone, punctuation, and clarity within your own drafted text
units.policy: The Editing, proofreading, and formatting category is checking grammar, tone, punctuation, and clarity in one's own text, creating citations and formatted documents, and converting formats, but not rewriting full paragraphs.

units.anchor: debugging code you wrote, having AI explain an algorithm or concept
units.policy: The Coding assistance category is debugging code one wrote, having AI explain an algorithm or concept, or generating sample code strictly for learning, for software and hardware description languages.

units.anchor: substantively rewriting portions of text or restructuring code you authored
units.policy: The Rewriting or refactoring category is substantively rewriting portions of text or restructuring code one authored.

units.anchor: using AI to generate conclusions or insights from a dataset
units.policy: The Analyzing data category is using AI to generate conclusions or insights from a dataset, or to set up, run, or interpret simulation and modeling outputs.

units.anchor: this is the highest-stakes category and is prohibited unless explicitly permitted by the instructor
units.policy: AI-generated work product (AI producing the primary submitted text, code, graphics, audio, or media) is prohibited unless explicitly permitted by the instructor or unless the output is itself the object of analysis.

units.anchor: These tiers indicate when AI use in research should be disclosed
units.policy: Appendix B tiers (adapted from Resnik and Hosseini, 2026) indicate when research AI use should be disclosed, absent stricter venue, funder, or IRB rules.

units.anchor: Where this table and venue rules differ, venue rules govern.
units.policy_type: NEW:Defer to external venue and sponsor rules

units.anchor: Formulate questions or hypotheses, or design and conduct experiments.
units.policy: Disclosure is mandatory when using AI to formulate questions or hypotheses, or to design and conduct experiments.

units.anchor: Draft parts of the paper, significantly revise, or synthesize text.
units.policy: Disclosure is mandatory when using AI to draft parts of the paper, significantly revise, or synthesize text.

units.anchor: Translate part or all of the paper.
units.policy: Disclosure is mandatory when using AI to translate part or all of the paper.

units.anchor: Collect, analyze, interpret, or visualize data (quantitative or qualitative).
units.policy: Disclosure is mandatory when using AI to collect, analyze, interpret, or visualize data.

units.anchor: Extract data for a literature review and identify knowledge gaps.
units.policy: Disclosure is mandatory when using AI to extract data for a literature review and identify knowledge gaps.

units.anchor: Generate synthetic data, images, or figures reported in the paper or used in the research.
units.policy: Disclosure is mandatory when using AI to generate synthetic data, images, or figures reported in or used for the research.

units.anchor: Find references, or verify the relevance of references found by a person.
units.policy: Disclosure is optional when using AI to find references or verify the relevance of references found by a person.

units.anchor: Find and generate examples for existing content.
units.policy: Disclosure is optional when using AI to find and generate examples for existing content.

units.anchor: Brainstorm or suggest how to organize a paper, or suggest a paper or section title.
units.policy: Disclosure is optional when using AI to brainstorm or suggest how to organize a paper or suggest a title.

units.anchor: Validate or give feedback on your own existing ideas, text, or code.
units.policy: Disclosure is optional when using AI to validate or give feedback on one's own existing ideas, text, or code.

units.anchor: Check grammar, spelling, punctuation, or formatting within your own drafted text.
units.policy: Disclosure is unnecessary when using AI to check grammar, spelling, punctuation, or formatting in one's own drafted text.

units.anchor: Search for sources or information.
units.policy: Disclosure is unnecessary when using AI to search for sources or information.

units.anchor: Suggest words or phrases that improve the clarity of an existing sentence.
units.policy: Disclosure is unnecessary when using AI to suggest words or phrases that improve the clarity of an existing sentence.

units.anchor: Perform autocomplete, or operate as a component in a larger system
units.policy: Disclosure is unnecessary when AI performs autocomplete or operates as a component in a larger system without generating content or making research decisions.

units.anchor: Act as a digital assistant, for example to organize and maintain a project's digital assets
units.policy: Disclosure is unnecessary when AI acts as a digital assistant, e.g., organizing a project's digital assets and workflows.

units.anchor: do not upload the document or its contents into non-approved AI tools for review assistance
units.policy: When reviewing manuscripts or grant proposals, do not upload the document or its contents into non-approved AI tools for review assistance.

units.anchor: Doing so breaches the confidentiality of unpublished work.
Both NSF and NIH prohibit GenAI use in its peer review process.
units.policy_type: NEW:Defer to external venue and sponsor rules

documents.unit: School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), graduate programs (ECE, CS, AI)
documents.title: EECS Graduate Handbook 2025-2026, Section 2.21 Guidelines for AI writing assistance and proper citation and attribution
documents.summary: Section 2.21 of the EECS graduate handbook (ECE, CS, AI programs) on AI writing assistance. It allows AI only to polish and correct grammar of content the student already created and forbids using AI to create new content or research. It recommends and, for examination-committee documents, requires a similarity check such as Draft Coach, and explains plagiarism and self-plagiarism risks.

units.anchor: acceptable to use AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) for writing assistance if a student uses them
units.policy: It is acceptable to use AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT) for writing assistance if a student uses them to polish and correct grammar of content already created.

units.anchor: may use AI tools to improve the writing and organization of that content created
units.policy: A student may use AI tools to improve the writing and organization of results and interpretations the student created.

units.anchor: the AI tool is just polishing the final 10%
units.policy: In acceptable use, the AI tool is just polishing the final 10% of the work.

units.anchor: Students may not use AI tools to create new content or research.
a student cannot ask ChatGPT to create an analysis or summary
units.policy: A student cannot ask ChatGPT to create an analysis or summary and then claim that text as their own writing.

units.anchor: ensure students are doing their own unique work and avoiding plagiarism issues
units.policy: The key issue is to ensure students are doing their own unique work and avoiding plagiarism issues.

units.anchor: Plagiarism is a serious offense with both short- and long-term consequences.
units.policy: Plagiarism is a serious offense with short- and long-term consequences; many careers have been ended by it.

units.anchor: they may create content that is effectively copied from another author
units.policy: Because AI tools draw from existing writing, they may create content that is effectively copied from another author.

units.anchor: it is recommended that students use Draft Coach
units.policy: Students are recommended to use Draft Coach (free via OSU's Google Docs and Microsoft 365) to check their work for similarity with other works, especially if an AI tool was involved.

units.anchor: This is especially important for conference and journal publications
units.policy: Similarity checking is especially important for conference and journal publications, since submissions are run through plagiarism checkers.

units.anchor: the organization generally acquires ownership of the contents
units.policy: When a student publishes with a professional society such as IEEE, the organization generally acquires ownership of the contents through a copyright agreement.

units.anchor: they can get flagged by a plagiarism checker, even though those are their own words
units.policy: Reusing one's own previously published text can be flagged by a plagiarism checker (self-plagiarism), even though the words are one's own.

units.anchor: It is the School's requirement that students perform due diligence
units.policy: The School requires students to perform this due diligence (similarity checking or equivalent) for all documents submitted to their examination committees.

units.anchor: they should check with their major advisor and/or with the AHGP
units.policy: Students with further questions about proper policy, attribution, or academic integrity should check with their major advisor and/or the AHGP.

new_types.name: Instructor AI for feedback and grading
new_types.definition: Instructors may use AI to give an initial review of student work, draft feedback, or score work against a rubric, under stated conditions (e.g., only approved tools, human review). Distinct from P46, which requires that humans assign the grades.

new_types.name: Instructor AI familiarity before policy
new_types.definition: Before writing a course AI policy, instructors should try AI tools themselves, learn their implications for teaching, and consult colleagues or unit leaders.

new_types.name: Defer to external venue and sponsor rules
new_types.definition: AI rules set by publication venues, funders, sponsors, IRBs, or industry partners take precedence over, or add restrictions beyond, the institution's own AI policy (mainly research and sponsored work).
